title: Before Dandadan, There Was Abenobashi: Remembering Anime's Forgotten Sleeper Hits
summary: Magical Shopping Arcade Abenobashi is the forgotten Gainax sleeper hit that walked so Dandadan could run. Let's look back at this 2002 classic and the golden age of ADV Films.
body:
Do you remember when anime in the West felt like the Wild West? If you were watching anime in the late '90s and early 2000s, you know exactly what I'm talking about.
We owe a massive debt to the true "grandfathers" of Western anime distribution — pioneers like ADV Films, Manga Entertainment, and Media Blasters (often remembered for their infamous Kitty Media label). These were the foundational companies that took massive risks to bring anime to where it is today. I honestly miss the presence that ADV Films had in the community. Their legacy is kept alive by Sentai Filmworks — born from the ashes of ADV — who continue to carry the torch for physical media and dubbing. But with the shift to modern streaming, we are slowly losing the memory of the absolute sleeper hits from that golden era.
Take Magical Shopping Arcade Abenobashi, for example.
Released in 2002 by Studio Gainax — the exact same visionary team that revolutionized the medium with Neon Genesis Evangelion and FLCL — this series is a forgotten masterpiece of pure, chaotic energy. It follows two kids from Osaka who get thrown into a string of parallel worlds, each one a brilliant, unhinged parody of a different genre: RPGs, sci-fi epics, dating sims, film noir, and classic kung fu cinema. It even features a phenomenal musical score by Shirō Sagisu — the legendary composer behind Evangelion.
If that formula sounds familiar — messy kids, reality constantly bending around them, slapstick comedy crashing headfirst into raw emotion — it should. It's exactly why Dandadan is such a massive hit today. Abenobashi was pulling off that same crazy energy more than 20 years earlier, even winning an Excellence Award at the Japan Media Arts Festival for its animation.
Unfortunately, Abenobashi is currently out of print and has largely faded into obscurity. But before we get completely absorbed by the latest seasonal hype, I wanted to shine a spotlight on this lost gem. We can't let the sleeper anime that helped build the culture we love today simply be forgotten.
If you've seen this classic — or if you manage to track it down before the next season of Dandadan hits — let me know your thoughts down below! (Side note: it's classic early-2000s Gainax, which means it can get a bit risqué. You've been warned!)
What are some of your favorite forgotten sleeper anime from the ADV Films era?

title: Who's Your Daddy? Joe Jackson as a Horror Icon
summary: After watching Michael, I went down a Joe Jackson rabbit hole. Three actors, three versions, one terrifying legacy. Left, Center or Right: which Joe would you have survived?
body:
If you had to grow up with one of these Joe Jacksons, who are you picking?

I just watched Michael, immediately threw on the 1992 miniseries The Jacksons: An American Dream, and then fell straight down a rabbit hole of real Joe Jackson interviews. By the end, I had one question: why isn't Joe Jackson talked about like a horror icon?

## Why Joe Jackson belongs in the horror portal

Think about what makes a great horror villain. He's in your house. You can't escape him. He decides when the day is over. And he has a signature weapon everybody recognizes.

For the Jackson kids, that was Joe and the belt.

That's not me being dramatic. Michael and his siblings talked for years about the beatings, the fear and rehearsals that never seemed to end. Joe defended it as discipline for the rest of his life. You can argue about whether that discipline built the Jackson 5, but you can't argue that it didn't scare them.

So here's the lineup.

## Left: Colman Domingo in Michael (2026)

Cinematic dread.

This is the big-screen, prestige-movie Joe, and the fear is in the atmosphere as much as in anything he does. You find yourself watching the kids' faces as much as you watch him, because you're waiting to see what happens next.

## Center: Lawrence Hilton-Jacobs in The Jacksons: An American Dream (1992)

The Enforcer. The Belt.

If you grew up in a house that watched this miniseries, you know exactly which version I mean. Hilton-Jacobs' Joe is the one a whole generation remembers: loud, hard and dead serious about getting those boys ready. It's '90s TV-event intensity, and it stuck with people.

## Right: the real Joe Jackson

The one who actually did it.

The real Joe built the Jackson 5 out of Gary, Indiana, with a work ethic and harsh discipline he never backed away from. Watching his real interviews after two dramatized versions is a different experience. There's no score, no lighting and no actor making choices. Just a man explaining why he did it, completely convinced he was right.

That's the scariest version, because it isn't a performance.

## My pick

TBH, I'd go with Hilton-Jacobs. I'd have fewer nightmares, but I'd still end up talented and famous.

## Update (September 2026)

Two things happened after I posted this.

First, Druski. While hosting the 2026 BET Awards at the end of June, he dropped a parody trailer called "Joe," a fake prequel to Michael, with Druski in heavy makeup as Joe Jackson, belt in hand, pushing his sons to the brink. It had the internet in tears, and some people felt it went too far with Janet Jackson and Jaafar Jackson in the building. For me, it was basically in line with everything in this post: when a comedian can build a whole horror-movie trailer out of Joe Jackson and everybody instantly gets the joke, that's a horror icon.

Second, Michael turned into a monster at the box office. It opened to about $97 million in the U.S., the best opening ever for a biopic, and went on to pass $1 billion worldwide, the first biopic to get there. Lionsgate's film chief has said there's "at least one more movie," and Colman Domingo has talked about a possible part two. So we might be getting more of Domingo's Joe.

Sources: [theGrio](https://thegrio.com/2026/06/29/druski-drops-new-joe-skit-while-hosting-the-bet-awards/), [Consequence](https://consequence.net/2026/06/druski-joe-jackson-michael-biopic-parody-sketch/), [Variety](https://variety.com/2026/film/box-office/michael-box-office-opening-weekend-record-1236730805/), [Screen Rant](https://screenrant.com/michael-jackson-biopic-sequel-update/)

## Quick answers

Who plays Joe Jackson in Michael? Colman Domingo, opposite Jaafar Jackson as Michael and Nia Long as Katherine Jackson.

Who played Joe Jackson in The Jacksons: An American Dream? Lawrence Hilton-Jacobs, in the 1992 miniseries.

What was Druski's Joe Jackson skit? A parody trailer called "Joe" that Druski debuted while hosting the 2026 BET Awards. It spoofs a dark prequel to Michael, with Druski playing Joe Jackson.

How much did Michael make at the box office? More than $1 billion worldwide, making it the highest-grossing biopic ever.

Is there going to be a Michael 2? Nothing's official yet, but Lionsgate's film chairman has said there's "at least one more movie."

title: Tales from the Crypt Is Back on Shudder — Do We Need a Remake?
summary: Almost 30 years after the Crypt Keeper closed the coffin, Tales from the Crypt is finally streaming on Shudder. Now the real question: do we need a remake, a reboot or a movie?
body:
Man, it's been a LONG time since I've seen the Crypt Keeper.

The last episode of Tales from the Crypt, "The Third Pig," aired back in 1996. That's almost 30 years since the show closed the coffin. And for most of that time, if you wanted to rewatch it, good luck.

Now it's finally streaming on Shudder, and I have to ask: do we need a new Tales from the Crypt?

## What made Tales from the Crypt special

Tales from the Crypt ran on HBO from 1989 to 1996: seven seasons of horror stories based on the EC Comics of the 1950s. Every episode was its own little nightmare, and most of them ended with somebody getting exactly what they deserved.

Hosting all of it was the Crypt Keeper, voiced by John Kassir: a cackling puppet corpse with a pun for everything. He was the reason you stayed for the ending. Horror comedy doesn't get much more iconic than that.

Being on HBO meant the show could go all out, too: real gore, practical effects and dark humor, with nothing cut for broadcast TV. And the guest list was ridiculous. Brad Pitt, Demi Moore, Michael J. Fox, Christopher Reeve, Kyle MacLachlan, Ewan McGregor, Steve Buscemi, Joe Pesci and Tim Curry all showed up at some point.

## Why it disappeared for so long

For years, Tales from the Crypt was one of the hardest classic horror shows to watch legally. It had never been on a streaming service. The rights were split between different companies and the people behind the original comics and the show, and nobody could get everything lined up.

That's also what killed the last attempt at bringing it back. In 2016, M. Night Shyamalan was set to revive Tales from the Crypt for TNT, and it fell apart over rights issues before it ever got made.

## Back on Shudder, uncut

Shudder started streaming Tales from the Crypt on May 1, 2026, beginning with season one and adding the rest every Friday through June 12. It's the first time the show has ever been on a streaming service, and all seven seasons are uncut and uncensored.

I'm glad it's back. A whole generation that never got to watch it on HBO can finally meet the Crypt Keeper.

## So, do we need a remake?

Here's where I'm torn.

The case for yes: anthology horror is perfect for right now. Short, nasty, standalone stories, practical effects and a host with personality. Horror fans would show up.

The case for no: the Crypt Keeper is John Kassir's voice and that specific puppet. A CGI Crypt Keeper or a gritty modern take would miss the whole point. The show worked because it was fun and mean at the same time.

If they do bring it back, keep the puppet, keep the puns and keep it R-rated. Otherwise, just let people discover the original on Shudder.

## Update (September 2026)

All seven seasons have been streaming uncut on Shudder since June 12. As of September, there's still no confirmed remake, reboot or movie.

Sources: [AMC Global Media](https://www.amcglobalmedia.com/2026/04/15/tales-from-the-crypt-streaming-for-the-first-time-exclusively-on-shudder/), [Bloody Disgusting](https://bloody-disgusting.com/tv/3949246/tales-from-the-crypt-now-streaming-for-the-very-first-time-on-shudder/), [Gizmodo](https://gizmodo.com/tales-from-the-crypt-streaming-shudder-2000745039)

## Quick answers

Where can I watch Tales from the Crypt? On Shudder. It's the first time the show has ever been available to stream, and all seven seasons are uncut.

When did Tales from the Crypt come to Shudder? Season one arrived May 1, 2026, and the rest rolled out weekly through June 12, 2026.

What was the last episode of Tales from the Crypt? "The Third Pig," which aired in 1996.

Who voices the Crypt Keeper? John Kassir.

Is there a Tales from the Crypt remake? Not as of September 2026. The last revival attempt, M. Night Shyamalan's series for TNT, fell apart over rights issues.

## Your turn

Do we need a new Tales from the Crypt? Remake, reboot or movie: yeah or nah? Tell me in the comments.

title: Not Every Book of the Dead Is the Same Kind of Curse
summary: Some guide the dead. Some weaponize the dead. Some reveal truths that break the mind. I split horror's Books of the Dead into 3 lanes. Which one is truly the worst?
body:
Not every Book of the Dead is the same kind of curse.

Some guide the dead. Some weaponize the dead. Some reveal truths that break the mind.

Horror keeps coming back to the same idea, an ancient book you should never open, but the books themselves are doing completely different jobs. So I split them into three lanes:

1. The Sacred Guide
2. Flesh-Bound Evil
3. Forbidden Cosmic Text

## Lane 1: The Sacred Guide

This is the one that's real. The ancient Egyptian Book of the Dead was never one single book. It was a collection of spells and instructions buried with the dead to help them make it through the afterlife. Its most famous moment is the weighing of the heart: your heart goes on a scale against the feather of Ma'at, and if it's heavy with wrongdoing, it gets devoured.

It was never meant to be a weapon. It's a map for the soul.

Horror still can't leave it alone, though. Movies like The Mummy turn it into something that brings the dead back instead of guiding them, because nothing's scarier than a sacred thing used wrong.

## Lane 2: Flesh-Bound Evil

This is the Evil Dead book: the Necronomicon Ex-Mortis, bound in human flesh and inked in blood. You read from it out loud, and you're not guiding the dead anywhere. You're inviting them into the living.

What comes next is possession. People you love turn into Deadites and taunt you in their own voices. It's direct, it's physical, and it happens right in front of you.

## Lane 3: Forbidden Cosmic Text

This is H.P. Lovecraft's Necronomicon, written by the "Mad Arab" Abdul Alhazred. It doesn't summon one demon to your cabin. It shows you the truth about the universe: ancient, uncaring cosmic beings, and how little humans matter to any of it.

Reading it doesn't possess your body. It breaks your mind. In Lovecraft's world, knowledge itself is the monster.

## Which one is the worst?

For me, Book 2 is the most instantly terrifying, because possession horror is direct. There's no confusion about what's happening. Something is inside the people around you, and it wants you.

But Book 3 might be worse long-term, because it's not just attacking your body. It's attacking your understanding of reality. You can fight a Deadite with a chainsaw. You can't un-learn what the Necronomicon tells you.

Book 1 is the only one I'd actually want to own. It's the only one designed to help you.

## Update (September 2026)

Lane 2 got bigger this summer. Evil Dead Burn came out in July, and this time the evil was already in the family's house: the Prices' grandfather, Benjamin, had been researching the Deadites and the Kandarian Dagger. And Evil Dead Wrath, a prequel set in 1972, is coming April 7, 2028.

For the full breakdown, read my [Evil Dead Burn review](articles/horror-evil-dead-burn-review-this-one-hits-different-and-not-how-yo.html) and [how the Burn leaks held up](articles/horror-evil-dead-burn-eyes.html).

Sources: [Wikipedia: Evil Dead Burn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evil_Dead_Burn), [Deadline on Evil Dead Wrath](https://deadline.com/2026/06/evil-dead-wrath-is-prequel-1236958743/)

## Quick answers

What is the Book of the Dead? The name covers a few very different books. The real Egyptian Book of the Dead was a collection of spells to guide the dead through the afterlife. In horror, it usually means the Evil Dead book or H.P. Lovecraft's Necronomicon.

Is the Necronomicon real? Not as an ancient book. Lovecraft invented it for his stories, and the Evil Dead movies created their own version.

What is the book in Evil Dead called? The Necronomicon Ex-Mortis, a book bound in human flesh and inked in blood.

What's the difference between Lovecraft's Necronomicon and the Evil Dead book? The Evil Dead book summons demons that possess people. Lovecraft's reveals cosmic truths that drive its readers insane.

## Your turn

Which Book of the Dead is the worst: the Sacred Guide, Flesh-Bound Evil or the Forbidden Cosmic Text? Tell me in the comments.

title: The Nightmare on Elm Street Mandela Effect Nobody Spotted
summary: For years I was sure Cathy Dennis's "Touch Me (All Night Long)" was in A Nightmare on Elm Street 2: Freddy's Revenge. It wasn't. The movie came out in 1985, and her version didn't exist until 1991. Turns out I created my own Mandela effect.
body:
For years, I was convinced Cathy Dennis's "Touch Me (All Night Long)" was in A Nightmare on Elm Street Part 2: Freddy's Revenge. I would've bet money on it.

I was wrong. And the way I got it wrong is kind of fascinating.

## How my brain rewrote a horror movie

I saw Freddy's Revenge as a kid once or twice, then didn't watch it again until the early 2000s. In between, I heard Cathy Dennis's version of "Touch Me (All Night Long)" so many times that my brain quietly stitched the two memories together.

So when I finally rewatched the movie, the song didn't sound like the version in my head. I was like, "What in the dream warrior is this?"

## The timeline doesn't lie

The dates make it impossible:

- Freddy's Revenge came out in 1985.
- Cathy Dennis's version came out in 1991.

The song in the movie is the original "Touch Me (All Night Long)" by Wish featuring Fonda Rae, from 1984. It's the track Jesse dances to in that famous scene where he's unpacking and cleaning up his room. Cathy Dennis's cover came six years after the movie.

My memory didn't just fade. It swapped in a recording that didn't even exist yet.

## Two versions, two different vibes

Both versions are bangers, but they don't have the same energy.

The Wish and Fonda Rae original is mid-'80s club music: synth-heavy, with Fonda Rae's big vocal out front. It reached number 5 on Billboard's dance club chart and number 49 in the UK.

Cathy Dennis's version is glossy early-'90s dance-pop, and it was a much bigger hit. It went to number 2 on the Billboard Hot 100 in May 1991 and number 1 on the dance club chart. That's the version that was all over the radio, which is exactly why it overwrote the original in my head.

## So is it really a Mandela effect?

A Mandela effect is usually a false memory that a lot of people share. I can't prove this one is widespread, which is why I'm asking. But on a personal level, it's the same thing: a confident memory built out of two different sources.

And it makes sense that it happened with this movie. Freddy's Revenge is the odd one out in the Nightmare series, and that dance scene is one of the most talked-about moments in it. A scene that memorable, paired with a song that later became a bigger hit in a different version, is the perfect setup for your brain to mix things up.

## Update (September 2026)

Freddy's coming back. In July, Paramount announced a new A Nightmare on Elm Street movie after making a deal with Wes Craven's estate for the U.S. rights. It's based on the original 1984 film and comes from Paramount Primal, the studio's new horror label run by J.D. Lifshitz and Raphael Margules, the producing team behind Barbarian and Weapons. Craven's widow, Iya Labunka, and his son, Jonathan Craven, are producing. There's no release date yet.

Sources: [Variety](https://variety.com/2026/film/news/nightmare-on-elm-street-reboot-paramount-wes-craven-estate-1236809749/), [The Hollywood Reporter](https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/movies/movie-news/nightmare-on-elm-street-movie-paramount-1236646496/), [Wikipedia: Touch Me (All Night Long)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Touch_Me_(All_Night_Long))

## Quick answers

What song is in A Nightmare on Elm Street 2: Freddy's Revenge? "Touch Me (All Night Long)" by Wish featuring Fonda Rae, the 1984 original, plays in the scene where Jesse dances while cleaning up his room.

Is Cathy Dennis's "Touch Me (All Night Long)" in Freddy's Revenge? No. Her cover came out in 1991, six years after the movie.

When did Freddy's Revenge come out? In 1985.

How high did Cathy Dennis's "Touch Me" chart? It reached number 2 on the Billboard Hot 100 in May 1991.

Is there a new Nightmare on Elm Street movie? Yes. Paramount announced one in July 2026, based on the 1984 original, but there's no release date yet.

## Your turn

Which version sounds right to you: Wish and Fonda Rae, or Cathy Dennis? And be honest: does the Cathy Dennis version feel more right than the original? Drop your answer in the comments.

title: XFD's Mount Rushmore of Legends: Romero, Toriyama, Hulk Hogan, Steve Jobs
summary: Horror: George Romero. Anime: Akira Toriyama. Wrestling: Hulk Hogan. Tech: Steve Jobs. I made the call. Now tell me who doesn't belong.
body:
I finally made my Mount Rushmore, and I already know somebody's getting replaced in the comments.

- Horror: George A. Romero
- Anime: Akira Toriyama
- Wrestling: Hulk Hogan
- Tech: Steve Jobs

My rule was simple: each one had to change their category in a major way. Not just be great at it. Change it.

## Horror: George A. Romero

Before Night of the Living Dead in 1968, movie zombies were mostly voodoo zombies, people under a spell. Romero turned them into the slow, hungry, flesh-eating dead that just keep coming, and every zombie movie, show and game since is standing on that.

He didn't stop there. Dawn of the Dead turned a shopping mall into a statement about consumerism, and Day of the Dead kept pushing. Romero used zombies to talk about society, and horror has been doing it ever since.

If you've watched The Walking Dead, played Resident Evil or seen any zombie movie at all, you've seen Romero's influence.

## Anime: Akira Toriyama

Dragon Ball changed everything. Goku became the blueprint for the shonen hero, and a huge part of the anime and manga that came after, from Naruto to One Piece, grew up in his shadow.

And Toriyama wasn't just Dragon Ball. He created Dr. Slump, and he designed the characters and monsters for Dragon Quest and the characters for Chrono Trigger, so his art shaped video games, too.

He passed in March 2024, and the whole world felt it.

## Wrestling: Hulk Hogan

Hulkamania took wrestling from a regional business to pop culture. Hogan main-evented the first WrestleMania, slammed André the Giant at WrestleMania III and became the face of the WWF boom in the '80s. Then he turned heel, joined the nWo in 1996 and helped WCW take over Monday nights.

Hogan is also the pick I expect the most heat on. Between the controversies later in his life and names like Stone Cold Steve Austin and The Rock, there's a real argument. But in terms of changing the category, the '80s boom doesn't happen without him. He died in July 2025.

## Tech: Steve Jobs

Apple, the Mac, the iPod, the iPhone. Jobs changed how normal people use technology, and then changed it again. The iPhone alone reshaped how everybody lives.

Bonus fact: Jobs bought the computer graphics group that became Pixar, and Pixar made Toy Story, the first fully computer-animated feature film. (If you read [my Toy Story 5 theory](articles/popculture-toy-story-5-is-actually-a-reboot-sequel.html), you know ReBoot got there first on TV.)

## Why these four

All four took something that already existed and changed what it meant. Romero redefined zombies. Toriyama redefined the shonen hero. Hogan made wrestling mainstream entertainment. Jobs made computers personal and phones essential.

But I know this list won't be safe.

## Update (September 2026)

These legacies are still making news:

- Romero: Twilight of the Dead, the long-planned final chapter of his zombie saga, is moving forward with Kate Beckinsale starring, the Paz brothers directing and the Romero estate on board.
- Toriyama: Dragon Ball Super is starting over this fall as Dragon Ball Super: Beerus, an enhanced version of the anime. He also worked on Dragon Ball Xenoverse 3 before he passed.
- Hogan: A biopic is back on the table. His son, Nick Hogan, said in April there's "absolutely potential" for a movie, after the earlier Netflix project with Chris Hemsworth and director Todd Phillips was dropped.

Sources: [Deadline](https://deadline.com/2026/05/kate-beckinsale-twilight-of-the-dead-movie-romero-1236904663/), [Dragon Ball official site](https://en.dragon-ball-official.com/news/01_3976.html), [Push Square](https://www.pushsquare.com/news/2026/04/akira-toriyama-worked-on-ps5s-dragon-ball-xenoverse-3-before-his-passing), [Fightful](https://www.fightful.com/wrestling/nick-hogan-says-hulk-hogan-biopic-is-still-possible/)

## Quick answers

Who is on XFD's Mount Rushmore? George A. Romero for horror, Akira Toriyama for anime, Hulk Hogan for wrestling and Steve Jobs for tech.

Why is George Romero so important to horror? His 1968 film Night of the Living Dead created the modern flesh-eating zombie that nearly every zombie story since has built on.

What did Akira Toriyama create? Dragon Ball and Dr. Slump, plus the character designs for Dragon Quest and Chrono Trigger.

Did Steve Jobs have anything to do with Toy Story? Yes. Jobs bought the computer graphics group that became Pixar, the studio that made Toy Story.

## Your turn

Who does NOT belong? And who would you put up there instead? Tell me in the comments.

title: Why 90s Practical Effects Still Hit Harder Than CGI
summary: A breakdown of why creature work, lighting, texture, and physical sets still make horror feel alive decades later. From Jurassic Park to Evil Dead, the practical effects era gave horror a weight CGI has never matched.
body:
The debate between practical effects and CGI never really ends in horror circles because the answer has always been obvious to anyone who grew up watching the right films. The Blob (1988). The Thing (1982). Evil Dead II. Jurassic Park. Tremors. These movies built tension and real fear out of foam, latex, hydraulics, and craftsmanship — and they still hold up because physical objects exist in real space in a way digital composites never fully can.

CGI gave filmmakers tools that practical effects couldn't match. Epic scale, impossible creatures, environments that would have cost a studio everything to build on set. That's legitimate. But the horror genre specifically lost something when it traded tactile weight for digital flexibility, and most mainstream horror has never gotten it back.

XFD makes the full case in the video — breaking down specific moments across eras where you can actually feel the difference between a creature that was physically in the room and one that was rendered in post. If you haven't seen these examples side by side, this one will change how you watch horror.

title: Evil Dead Burn: Every Alleged Leak From Those L.A. Test Screenings (And What's Actually Real)
summary: The L.A. test-screening leaks were everywhere: a Deadite dog, a homemade Necronomicon and a flaming final boss. I sorted what looked confirmed from what was fan fiction in a trench coat, then checked the scorecard after release.
body:
⚠ MASSIVE SPOILER WARNING. I'm about to gut this thing open. If you want Evil Dead Burn to hit you cold in the theater, close the tab now. Still here? Good. Let's get nasty.

Evil Dead Burn hits theaters July 10, and the internet's been on fire (pun absolutely intended) ever since Reddit users who caught early Fangoria test screenings in Los Angeles started posting major plot details. Reactions from those screenings are mixed. Some people are comparing it to Evil Dead Rise, and others say they still prefer Army of Darkness.

A lot of what's floating around lines up with legit reporting. Some of it is fan fiction wearing a trench coat. So I went through the big ones and gave each one a verdict. Grab your boomstick.

## The tone: mean, nasty and zero slapstick

The first thing screeners agree on: this is not Army of Darkness. There's reportedly no slapstick comedy at all. Fans are calling it a mean, nasty, New French Extremity–style nightmare. If you know that corner of horror, that means director Sébastien Vaniček came to make you deeply uncomfortable and leave you there.

Verdict: confirmed vibe. It matches everything Vaniček has said in interviews.

## A possessed Deadite dog

This one's new for the franchise: a brutal scene with a possessed Deadite dog. Evil Dead has flirted with possessed animals before (that cackling deer head in Evil Dead II doesn't count), but a full demon dog in a mainline theatrical entry would be a first.

Verdict: confirmed.

## Jessica, the car crash and Will

Burn reportedly picks up Jessica's story from the cabin at the lake at the start of Evil Dead Rise. She appears to cause the car crash that kills Will, the husband of our lead, Alice. That loss is why Alice ends up at her in-laws' remote family home.

But according to the leaks, the attack may not be as random as it looks.

Verdict: confirmed.

## The 2013 connection and a homemade Necronomicon

Here's where it gets good for the lore hounds. The story reportedly connects to Fede Álvarez's 2013 Evil Dead. Will's grandfather was an occult investigator who tracked down the Kandarian Dagger and kept newspaper articles about the 2013 cabin massacre. He also made his own DIY journal based on the Necronomicon.

My theory: the Kandarian demons are being drawn to that journal. Either they're out for revenge against the family, or they're fulfilling a bigger prophecy in the Evil Dead universe.

Verdict: the grandfather and the Dagger look confirmed. The revenge-or-prophecy part is my speculation.

## The unfinished incantation

Allegedly, Alice finds the journal and starts reading the incantation without finishing it. So instead of giving the dead permission to possess the living, she may have just told them where the journal is.

That's a throwback to Army of Darkness, when Ash doesn't finish the words in the graveyard scene. Klaatu, barada... necktie.

Verdict: unverified plot detail. Treat it as a leak.

## The Inferno Deadite final boss

Toward the end of the movie, Will is resurrected as the Inferno Deadite, the final boss. He's described as a constantly burning host, reportedly done with real practical fire effects. Nice.

Alice going up against the burning body of the husband she's still grieving is the kind of emotional gut-punch this franchise doesn't usually swing for.

Verdict: confirmed.

## The post-credits scene rumor

Here's where it gets sketchy. People at the test screenings claim the director pulled the post-credits scene from the showing to prevent spoilers. Attendees think it features a major character returning, possibly a woman, based on how hard Burn leans on the 2013 storyline.

That's why I'm going with Mia, the survivor of the 2013 cabin massacre. Beth, the survivor of Evil Dead Rise, is the other name going around.

Verdict: can't be verified. Fun to chew on. Don't tattoo it on yourself.

## My bottom line before release

Strip away the post-credits rumor, and what's left sounds genuinely vicious: practical gore, real fire, a demon dog, a homemade Book of the Dead and a final boss built to break your heart before it breaks your body. If the screeners are right, Vaniček understood the assignment and then set the assignment on fire.

## Update (September 2026): how the leaks held up

Burn came out July 10 (Warner Bros. actually moved it up from July 24), so here's the scorecard.

Right:

- The tone. The Rotten Tomatoes critics' consensus literally calls it "the meanest, nastiest, and ickiest chapter."
- The Deadite dog. His name is Max.
- Jessica and the crash. A possessed Jessica causes the crash that turns Will into a Deadite.
- The grandfather and the Kandarian Dagger. Will's brother Joseph finds their grandfather Benjamin's research on the Deadites and the Dagger.
- The burning final boss. Alice's last fight is against a charred Deadite Will, with real practical fire.

Wrong:

- Alice doesn't botch the incantation. The words from the Necronomicon are recited by the possessed Jessica.

Half right:

- The post-credits scene. There are actually two. In the first, Polly escapes by cutting off her own leg and attacks a passing driver. In the second, Deadite Ellie Bixler from Evil Dead Rise comes back at the crematorium holding her ashes. So a major female character does return, just not Mia or Beth.

Couldn't confirm:

- The newspaper clippings about the 2013 cabin massacre. I haven't seen that detail confirmed anywhere reliable.

And one call that held up: I said the door was open for Evil Dead Wrath, the 1972 prequel. It's still coming, from writer-director Francis Galluppi, on April 7, 2028.

Burn made about $72.3 million worldwide on a $20 million budget. My full thoughts are in my [Evil Dead Burn review](articles/horror-evil-dead-burn-review-this-one-hits-different-and-not-how-yo.html).

Sources: [Wikipedia: Evil Dead Burn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evil_Dead_Burn), [Screen Rant on the post-credits scenes](https://screenrant.com/evil-dead-burn-post-credits-scene-sebastien-vanicek/), [Deadline on Evil Dead Wrath](https://deadline.com/2026/06/evil-dead-wrath-is-prequel-1236958743/)

## Quick answers

Is Evil Dead Burn connected to Evil Dead Rise? Yes. It's a direct sequel that brings back Jessica, the Deadite from the lake-cabin opening of Rise.

Does Evil Dead Burn have a dog? Yes. A possessed Deadite dog named Max.

Who is the final boss in Evil Dead Burn? Will, Alice's husband, who comes back as a burning, charred Deadite, filmed with practical fire effects.

How many post-credits scenes does Evil Dead Burn have? Two. One follows Polly's escape, and the other brings back Ellie Bixler from Evil Dead Rise.

Is Mia in Evil Dead Burn? No. The fan theory that Mia returns after the credits turned out to be wrong.

When does Evil Dead Wrath come out? April 7, 2028. It's a prequel set in 1972.

## Your turn

Which leak did you believe, and which one fooled you? Tell me in the comments.

title: Sony Ends Physical PlayStation Games in 2028 — Nintendo's About to WIN
summary:
Sony just confirmed it — new PlayStation games go 100% digital starting January 2028. No more discs. And I don't think they thought this all the way through. 🎮❌

In this one I break down why this isn't just a collector problem — it's a retail problem. Walmart, GameStop, Target, Best Buy… they all lose when physical games die. And when you can't actually OWN what you buy anymore? That's a scary road.

My money? Nintendo's about to step up and take the throne. But I wanna know where YOU land.
body:
Sony just said the quiet part out loud: starting January 2028, new PlayStation games go all-digital. No discs. No case on the shelf. No "hey, borrow this for the weekend." Just a license sitting on a server somewhere and a whole lot of trust.

And look — we get the business math. We just don't think anybody in that boardroom followed the thread all the way to the end.

## You Don't Own It. You Never Did.

Here's the part that should make you sit up. When you buy a digital game, you are not buying a game. You're buying permission to play one, and that permission belongs to whoever runs the store.

That's not doom-posting, that's documented. Digital movie libraries have already had titles yanked when licensing deals expired. Storefronts for older consoles have closed and taken their catalogs down with them. The pattern never changes: the servers go dark, and the thing you paid for stops existing.

A disc never asked you to trust anybody. It worked because it was in your hand. Kill that, and every game you "own" is only as permanent as the company's next licensing meeting.

## The Part Nobody's Talking About: Retail Bleeds Too

This isn't just a collector problem. It's a retail problem, and it's bigger than gaming.

Physical game sales are what walk people through the door at:

- GameStop
- Walmart
- Target
- Best Buy

And nobody walks into a store for exactly one thing. You come in for a $70 game and you leave with a controller, a headset, a gift card, a Funko you absolutely did not need. That disc is the reason the rest of the cart happens.

Take discs off the shelf and you don't just delete a product line — you delete the foot traffic that funds the entire gaming section. GameStop especially is staring down a future where a huge chunk of its reason to exist evaporates on a date Sony picked without them.

## Which Is Exactly Where Nintendo Walks In

PlayStation has been on top long enough to start believing it can't fall off. That's usually right about when it happens.

Because every player Sony pushes away has to land somewhere. Collectors. Preservationists. Parents who want something physical to actually wrap. Anybody on bad internet. Anybody who's just tired of paying full price for a file that can be switched off.

Nintendo still ships cartridges. Nintendo still hands you a thing you can hold, lend, resell, and keep in a drawer for fifteen years. If Sony spends 2028 telling a whole segment of its own audience they're not welcome anymore, Nintendo doesn't have to go win them — it just has to leave the door open.

Market dominance is rented, not owned. Ask Blockbuster.

## Great Margins, Shame About the Trust

To be fair, the corporate case is airtight on paper. No discs means no manufacturing, no shipping, no shelf space, no used market undercutting your price, and total control over what everything costs forever. Every quarterly report gets prettier.

But margin isn't the same thing as health. You can optimize a business right past the point where anybody actually likes it. Sony didn't get here on hardware specs alone — it got here on decades of goodwill from players who bought in early and stayed loyal. Goodwill is the one asset that never shows up on a balance sheet and never comes back once you've spent it.

## The XFD Bottom Line

This was never really about discs. It's about whether "buy" still means buy — or whether it quietly turned into "rent, indefinitely, until we decide otherwise."

January 2028 is the deadline Sony set for itself. Between now and then, the only vote that actually lands is the one you make with your wallet.

So where do you stand? Ready to go all-digital, or are you holding the line on physical? Tell us — we're reading every one.

title: The Season of Metal Is HERE 🔩 Metal Sonic Takes Shadow's Throne | Sonic 4 & New Anime
summary:
They handed Shadow the crown… but Metal Sonic was Sonic's FIRST true rival back in 1993 — a good 8 years before Shadow even existed. And 2026? This is the year my boy FINALLY gets his roses: main villain of the anime short Memories and Beyond this fall, AND the Final Boss of Sonic 4 in theaters March 2027.

The OG is taking his throne back. It's our time to shine. Welcome to the Season of Metal. 🔩
body:
Let's get one thing straight before we start: Shadow the Hedgehog is not Sonic's original rival. He's the popular one. There's a difference, and 2026 is finally about to prove it.

## 1993 Called. It Wants Its Bloodline Back.

Metal Sonic showed up in Sonic CD in 1993 and invented the entire idea — the cold, perfect copy built to be everything Sonic is, minus the heart. Same speed. Same shape. None of the soul. That's the blueprint every evil-double character since has been working from.

Shadow doesn't exist until 2001. Eight years later. Eight. By the time the ultimate lifeform got his big dramatic entrance, Metal had already been running the dark-mirror lane since the Genesis days.

And then Sega handed the crown to the new guy anyway.

## How Shadow Ran Off With the Crown

Credit where it's due, Shadow earned his spot. He got:

- His own solo game, guns and all
- The tragic backstory that made a whole generation feel things
- A live-action debut that walked off with the entire third movie
- Two straight decades as the face of "mature" Sonic

Metal Sonic got boss fights. Great boss fights — but boss fights. He'd turn up, wreck your afternoon, and vanish until somebody remembered he was cool.

That's the part that always stung. The character who built the rival lane spent twenty years parked in it.

## The Season of Metal Starts Now

Here's why we're calling 2026 the year it flips. Metal isn't getting one bone thrown his way. He's getting two, and they're both enormous.

First, the anime short: Memories and Beyond. Metal Sonic is the main villain, and the setup is genuinely nasty — Eggman goes after Sonic's life data and the Chaos Emeralds, then pours both into building something that shouldn't be able to exist. Not a copy of how Sonic moves. A copy of who Sonic is, wearing Chaos energy like armor. That one lands this fall.

Second, Sonic 4. Jeff Fowler confirmed it: Metal Sonic is the final boss. Not a mid-film obstacle, not a wink in a post-credits stinger — the last fight of the movie. In theaters March 2027.

Villain of the anime and final boss of the film, inside the same twelve months. That's not fan service. That's a coronation.

## Why This Version of Metal Actually Hits Different

The Eggman plan in Memories and Beyond is the smartest thing anybody's done with this character in years, because it quietly fixes his one real weakness.

Metal Sonic has always been the copy that can't close the gap. He's got the speed and the strength, but never the thing that makes Sonic win anyway. Hand him Sonic's actual life data and Chaos Emerald power on top of it, and the gap isn't there anymore. You're not fighting a knockoff. You're fighting yourself with the safety off.

Shadow's threat was always emotional — he's the guy who might not save you. Metal's threat is existential — he's the guy who proves you were replaceable the whole time.

## The XFD Bottom Line

Shadow had a hell of a run and nobody's taking that away from him. But the OG is stepping back into the light with an anime villain slot and a movie final boss in the same year, and the 1993 bloodline is finally getting its roses.

Welcome to the Season of Metal. 🔩

So settle it for us — Team Metal or Team Shadow?

title: Evil Dead Burn Review — This One Hits Different (And Not How You Think)
summary:
Evil Dead Burn is here, and it's a bloody good time — but it also made something impossible to ignore. Six movies in, there's no chosen one to tie it all together. Just survivors. In this review I break down what the new era gets consistently right (the Deadites eat), the return that left me disappointed, the fan-favorite elements the old series had that these new ones are missing, and the Bruce Campbell cameo hiding on the wall — and no y'all, he's NOT playing Ash.

Do you miss the old series with Ash, or do you like the new Deadite experience?
body:
Evil Dead Burn is here, and it's a really fun movie. But these new Evil Dead movies are trying to tell us something, y'all: we can't have any family reunions. I feel like somebody was watching Madea's Family Reunion and said, "What if we add Evil Dead into the mix?"

Six movies in, Burn also made something impossible to ignore. There's no chosen one tying this franchise together anymore. Just survivors.

## What Evil Dead Burn gets right

Let me give it its flowers first, because it earns them.

- The action is intense, and it doesn't let up.
- The gore goes hard, and the practical effects still land. There's more CGI in this one than in the last two, and you'll notice it, but when the real stuff shows up, it hits.
- The Deadites are center stage, right where they belong.

That last one matters most. Just like the 2013 Evil Dead and Evil Dead Rise, Burn has some really great moments with the Deadites. That specific kind of wrong, something wearing the face of somebody you love and enjoying it, is fully intact. If there's one thing this new era gets right every single time, it's the Deadites.

If you came for a nasty night at the movies, you're getting one.

## The chosen one problem

Here's what hit me on the way out.

This movie made something more noticeable than the other two did: there's no sense of a chosen one tying them together. Every entry in the new era runs the same shape. Ordinary people, one terrible night, somebody they love turns into something else, and whoever's left tries to make it to sunrise.

It works, and it's scary. But nobody carries you from one movie into the next, and six movies in, you feel that hole.

## The return that let me down

Y'all probably already know that someone returns from the previous film. I won't spell it out for anybody who hasn't seen it yet, but I'll be honest: I was a bit disappointed.

And that's what made me realize how much this new series is missing the fan-favorite elements that made the original run so beloved.

## What the old Evil Dead had that the new era doesn't

Remember when Evil Dead was this?

- A Farewell to Arms. Ash cuts off his own possessed hand in Evil Dead II, traps it under a bucket and stacks books on top, with that one sitting right there.
- Having a conversation with yourself in the mirror about what happened to your girlfriend.
- Being that guy with the gun. This is my boomstick.
- Having a bunch of mini-mes trying to take you out in Army of Darkness.

That was Evil Dead. Horror and slapstick at the same time, with one unforgettable guy in the middle of all of it.

Now it's mostly wolves in familiar clothing. "Mommy's with the maggots now." It's effective, and Rise is a great movie, but it's a completely different identity.

## Bruce Campbell is in it (kind of)

Yes, Bruce Campbell is in Evil Dead Burn. He has a cameo as one of the photos on the wall, watching over the family like, "You got this, right?"

He is not playing Ash in this one, y'all. It's very confusing. Campbell has even shot down the fan theory that his photo is supposed to be the family's grandfather. Love it or hate it, that's classic Evil Dead for you.

## How the leaks held up

Before release, I went through [every alleged leak from the L.A. test screenings](articles/horror-evil-dead-burn-eyes.html) and sorted what looked real from the fan fiction. Now that the movie's out, most of the big ones landed, but not all of them. That article has the full scorecard.

## Update (September 2026)

Here's how Burn did after this review went up:

- Box office: It opened in fourth place with about $13.7 million and finished around $72.3 million worldwide, on a reported $20 million budget.
- Reviews: It sits at about 71% on Rotten Tomatoes, where the critics' consensus calls it "the meanest, nastiest, and ickiest chapter." Audiences gave it a B CinemaScore.
- Stay through the credits: Burn has two post-credits scenes. I break both of them down in the leaks article.
- What's next: Evil Dead Wrath, from writer-director Francis Galluppi, is a prequel set in 1972, due in theaters April 7, 2028.

Sources: [Wikipedia: Evil Dead Burn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evil_Dead_Burn), [Deadline on Evil Dead Wrath](https://deadline.com/2026/06/evil-dead-wrath-is-prequel-1236958743/)

## Quick answers

Is Evil Dead Burn good? Yes. It's a fun, brutal horror movie with intense action, strong practical gore and great Deadites, even with more CGI than the last two films.

Is Bruce Campbell in Evil Dead Burn? Only as a cameo in a photo on the wall. He doesn't play Ash.

Is Ash in Evil Dead Burn? No. The new era follows ordinary families instead of a chosen-one hero like Ash Williams.

Does Evil Dead Burn have a post-credits scene? Yes, it has two, so stay through the credits.

What's the next Evil Dead movie? Evil Dead Wrath, a prequel set in 1972, due in theaters April 7, 2028.

title: Resident Evil (2026) Review — The Rat Guy & The Ending
summary:
Zach Cregger's Resident Evil is the best-reviewed movie in franchise history — and I had a blast. But two moments took me out: the sewer rat guy and the ending. And it turns out Cregger said this was going to be his Evil Dead II, then cut the jokes after test screenings. That explains a lot.

⚠️ Ending spoilers after the warning card.

How should the ending have gone? Best rewrite in the comments gets featured in the next video.
body:
The short version: Zach Cregger's Resident Evil is a banger. It's fast, it's scary, it's funny in the right places, and it's the most fun I've had with this franchise in a theater in years. But it doesn't always feel like Resident Evil, and when it ends, it just… ends. XFD Rating: B+. Ending not included.

## A Resident Evil movie with no Resident Evil heroes

Let's get this out of the way first, because it's the question every fan walks in with: no, Leon isn't in it. Neither are Jill, Chris, Claire, Ada or Wesker. If you're buying a ticket hoping to see your favorite character on the big screen, this one isn't for you, and the movie doesn't lean on them at all.

Instead, Resident Evil (2026) follows Bryan (Austin Abrams), a medical courier who takes one more delivery before heading home because it pays double. That delivery takes him into Raccoon City right as the outbreak breaks loose. Hazard pay, in the most literal way possible. (In Japan the games are called Biohazard. You see it.)

The story runs alongside the events of Resident Evil 2, but it's set in the present day and it's its own thing. Director Zach Cregger (Barbarian, Weapons), who co-wrote it with Shay Hatten, has been open about that choice. He said he wanted his lead to be "more of an Ethan than a Leon," a nod to Ethan Winters from Resident Evil 7 and Village: a regular guy with no special skills who, in Cregger's words, would "miss like 90 percent of the shots he takes with a gun."

And honestly? That part works.

## What works: an everyman in the wrong place at the wrong time

Bryan isn't a hero. He's a dude who just wants to go home, and he spends the whole movie trying to. That makes every scare land harder, because you're not watching a trained soldier clear a room. You're watching somebody who has no business being there try not to die.

The action is constant. The jump scares hit. The pacing never drags. At its best, it feels like the early-2000s Resident Evil movies I grew up going to see in theaters: loud, a little ridiculous, and a whole lot of fun.

The critics agree. The film opened to 96% on Rotten Tomatoes, a B+ CinemaScore (the best the franchise has ever gotten), and a $60 million opening weekend, the biggest in the series' history. Welcome to Raccoon City sat at 30% on Rotten Tomatoes. Whatever you think of the ending, this is the best-received Resident Evil movie ever made.

I had a blast. I want to be clear about that before I get into the rest.

## What doesn't: familiar, and not always Resident Evil

Here's my honest problem. Wrong-place-wrong-time survival horror is a great setup, but it's also one we've seen a lot. Take the Raccoon City name off this movie and you've still got a solid horror flick, just not one that does anything the genre hasn't done before.

And at times, I forgot I was watching a Resident Evil movie. The pieces are there: Raccoon City, Umbrella scientists, the sewers, a final transformation that's a clear nod to William Birkin from Resident Evil 2. But I didn't feel the connection. It had the parts of the games without the pull of them.

Then there are two moments that took me all the way out.

## The rat guy (mild spoilers)

Bryan drops into the sewers and finds a pale man just… sitting there. His stomach opens up and rats pour out of him, everywhere.

My questions:

- How did the rats get in him?
- That many?
- And was he just sitting down there waiting for somebody to walk by?

That's not a movie scene. That's a video game boss level. Everything up to that point had been grounded, a regular guy in a real city falling apart, and suddenly the movie asks you to accept something with zero logic behind it. It broke the realism the film had spent all that time building.

## The receipts: why it happened

This part surprised me. It turns out the rat guy might not be a mistake so much as a leftover.

Cregger said early on that Resident Evil was going to be his Evil Dead II: "a rock 'em, sock 'em… it's for me to play. And turn my brain off and just make an… Evil Dead 2… get crazy with the camera."

Then the test screenings happened. As Cregger told The Hollywood Reporter: "People really liked the movie, but they thought it was too funny." So he "stripped out as much of the jokes as possible."

And that explains a lot. In Evil Dead II, you never stop to ask how anything works. The movie is in on the joke, and the tone covers it. Cregger kept the wild set pieces but cut the comedy that would have made them make sense.

He kept the rat guy. He cut the movie that made the rat guy make sense.

That's my read on it, not something Cregger has said directly. But the timeline lines up.

## ⚠️ SPOILERS: the ending

Skip to "Why the Alice movies hooked me" if you haven't seen it.

Everybody catches stupid at the exact same time.

Bryan gets bitten in the tunnel while trying to help an infected girl, and he hides it. The scientists walk him right into the lab anyway. He mutates into the thing, the cure he spent the whole movie carrying falls twenty stories off a sky bridge, and nobody ever brings it up again. The last thing we see is Bryan, now a monster, turning toward the National Guard helicopters and roaring.

Roll credits.

We spent the entire movie with this guy, and he doesn't even get to go out as himself. No hint of what's next. No tease. No thread to pull.

And that's what gets me most. Even the games give you an ending. Resident Evil 2 doesn't stop the second you beat Birkin. You escape, you get an epilogue, you get a setup for what comes next. This movie ends on the boss fight and skips everything after.

## Why the Alice movies hooked me

Here's where I have to be upfront about my history with this series.

Back in the day, I played the Resident Evil games, but I wasn't really a fan. I didn't have much access to them, and my heart belonged to JRPGs. That was my escape. Where I really connected with Resident Evil was the movies.

Every time a new one came out, I was in a theater seat having a good time. And the thing that kept me coming back was simple: the stories were connected, and there was always something to look forward to.

The end of the first Resident Evil (2002) is a perfect example. Alice wakes up in a hospital, walks outside, and Raccoon City is gone. It's destroyed and empty. I walked out of that movie needing to know what happened next. It gave me hope, and it gave me a reason to come back.

And here's the thing a lot of people forget: Alice wasn't from the games either. Milla Jovovich's character was created for the movies. Those films proved you don't need Leon to make a Resident Evil movie people love.

So my problem with the 2026 movie isn't that it doesn't have Leon.

It's that it doesn't have an Alice.

It doesn't have someone to follow into the next one. Bryan's story starts and ends in the same two hours, and when the credits roll there's nothing left to hope for.

I said the same thing about [Evil Dead Burn](article.html?id=horror-evil-dead-burn-review-this-one-hits-different-and-not-how-yo): there's no chosen one tying it all together anymore, just survivors. Resident Evil just joined that club.

## Where does the series go from here?

This is the part I can't figure out, and I don't think anyone can yet.

Nothing's been announced. Cregger has said he "can't help thinking about other places this story could go," and a record-breaking opening usually means more movies are coming. But what comes next? (Everything from here on is my speculation.)

That's the catch with this movie's success. It proved a Resident Evil movie can be a hit without the video game characters. Which is great for the studio, but it also means there's no built-in road map anymore. No "Leon's next," no "Alice returns." The next film could be anything, and after this ending, I have no idea what I'm supposed to be waiting for.

## Every Resident Evil movie, ranked

Here's where the new one lands among the rest. This is my list, from a guy who saw most of these in theaters.

1. Resident Evil (2002) — Where it all started. Alice, the Red Queen, the laser hallway, and one of the best "what happens next?" endings in any horror movie. Still the one.

2. Resident Evil: Apocalypse (2004) — Raccoon City falling apart, Jill Valentine, and Nemesis. It took that cliffhanger and paid it off.

3. Resident Evil (2026) — The most fun I've had with the series in years. It would be higher if it gave me a reason to come back.

4. Resident Evil: Retribution (2012) — It makes the list mainly for one reason: Rain came back. Michelle Rodriguez's return was worth the ticket by itself.

5. Resident Evil: The Final Chapter (2016) — Back to the Hive to close out Alice's story. It gave the saga an ending, which is more than I can say for the new one.

6. Resident Evil: Welcome to Raccoon City (2021) — The one that finally put Claire, Chris, Jill and Leon on screen together in the 1998 setting.

7. Resident Evil: Extinction (2007) — The desert road-trip entry, with Claire Redfield joining the fight.

8. Resident Evil: Afterlife (2010) — The 3D one, with Chris Redfield and Wesker. Bottom of my list.

Disagree? I know some of y'all are ready to fight me over Afterlife. Tell me your ranking in the comments.

## So, is Resident Evil (2026) worth watching?

Yes. Go see it in theaters. It's loud, it's scary, it's a great crowd movie, and it's going to be all over everybody's Halloween watchlist this year and every year after, just like the old ones.

Just go in knowing what it is: a great one-time ride, not the start of a saga. Enjoy the everyman, enjoy the scares, and don't wait for Leon to show up.

XFD Rating: B+. Ending not included.

## Quick answers

Is Resident Evil (2026) worth watching? Yes, as a fun one-time theater watch and a Halloween pick. Longtime fans hoping for game characters or a connected story may be let down.

Is Leon, Jill or Chris in it? No. The lead is an original character, Bryan, a medical courier played by Austin Abrams.

Is it connected to the Milla Jovovich movies? No. It's a fresh start set in Raccoon City in the present day, running alongside the events of Resident Evil 2.

Will there be a sequel? Nothing's announced. Cregger says he's thought about where the story could go, and the record opening makes more movies likely, but that's speculation for now.

Who directed it? Zach Cregger (Barbarian, Weapons), who co-wrote it with Shay Hatten.

title: Toy Story 5 is Actually a ReBoot Sequel
summary:
Everyone thinks Pixar's 1995 Toy Story was the first to do 3D, but a 1994 Canadian cartoon called ReBoot beat them to it. And here's the wild part: they are secretly the exact same story.

From the kids (Andy and the User) abandoning their worlds, to the dark turn in Season 4 of ReBoot, to the Toys vs. Tech plot in Toy Story 5 — this is a crossover 30 years in the making. Follow, or get rebooted.
body:
Everybody gives Pixar's Toy Story the credit for being the first 3D cartoon. It wasn't. Not even close. Something beat it by more than a year, and the wild part is that it's secretly the same story, all the way up to Toy Story 5.

## ReBoot beat Toy Story by over a year

ReBoot premiered in September 1994, a Canadian show that aired Saturday mornings on YTV and ABC. It was the first fully computer-animated TV series ever made. Toy Story didn't hit theaters until November 1995. Pixar got the first CGI feature film, but ReBoot got there first.

## Mainframe and the User

Inside a computer lives a city called Mainframe. Every time a kid loads up a game, it drops on that city like a bomb.

Because to everybody in Mainframe, the kid at the keyboard is a god. They call him the User, and they can't agree on him:

- Some look up to him.
- Some blame him for the viruses.
- Some think he isn't even real, just a story somebody made up to keep everybody in line.

## Andy's toys live by the same rules

Swap the computer for a kid's bedroom and you've got Toy Story. Don't move. Don't get seen. Live for the kid. And just like the Mainframe doubters, Buzz spends the whole first movie refusing to believe he's a toy at all.

## Where the two stories split

This is where ReBoot goes darker. In Mainframe, the User drops a game, loads himself in as a character, and the programs have to beat him. If he wins, everyone caught in that game gets wiped out. If he loses, they get to see another day.

Same kind of god. Way higher price.

## When the kids grew up, both worlds paid for it

Andy trades his toys for camp, a cell phone and friends, then college and adulthood.

The User moves on to darker games, and he wins one. It costs Enzo, Mainframe's wide-eyed kid, his eye and his innocence. He comes back as Matrix, and the whole system has to crash and reboot just to survive.

## Two worlds abandoned by gods who never knew they existed

Then both gods leave.

Andy donates his toys to Bonnie, and Woody has to figure out life without him. In ReBoot, by the final two episodes the User's keyboard is just dead. Mainframe goes dark for nearly 20 years, until the 2018 sequel, ReBoot: The Guardian Code, reveals him as a grown man-child buried under ReBoot merch in his mom's basement.

Two worlds, abandoned by gods who never knew they existed.

## The wildest part is what happened in real life

The story is wild. Reality is wilder.

Toy Story got five movies and billions at the box office. ReBoot got the opposite. The House of Mouse dropped it as soon as Disney bought ABC. YTV and Toonami kept it alive for more seasons until the money ran dry, and Season 4 got cut down to eight episodes.

So they rewrote the ending into a cliffhanger on purpose. Megabyte wins. Game over.

This show spent seven years telling a story about a world left behind by its god, and then it became one. The creator still holds the true ending, in case he ever gets to finish it.

## Both worlds saved themselves

Andy didn't come to that incinerator in Toy Story 3. Mainframe fought Megabyte with nobody at the keyboard. In both worlds, when it counted most, the god wasn't there, so they saved themselves.

## Toy Story 5 brings it full circle

In Toy Story 5, the toys finally clash with technology itself, going up against tech like Lilypad, a tablet that would fit right in inside Mainframe. By the end, they learn how to coexist.

So the next time some jabroni calls Toy Story 5 just another sequel, tell them it's a crossover 30 years in the making.

## Quick answers

Was Toy Story the first 3D cartoon? No. ReBoot premiered in September 1994 as the first fully computer-animated TV series, more than a year before Toy Story (November 1995), which was the first fully computer-animated feature film.

What is ReBoot about? It's set in Mainframe, a city inside a computer. When the User loads a game, the programs have to beat him inside it, or everyone caught in the game gets wiped out.

Who is the User in ReBoot? The person at the keyboard. To the people of Mainframe he's a god. Some worship him, some blame him, and some don't believe he's real.

Why did ReBoot end on a cliffhanger? The money ran out. Season 4 was cut to eight episodes, so the ending was rewritten into a cliffhanger on purpose, with Megabyte winning.

Is there a ReBoot sequel? Yes. ReBoot: The Guardian Code came out in 2018.

What is Toy Story 5 about? Toys versus tech. The toys clash with technology like Lilypad, a tablet, and learn to coexist with it.

## Your turn

Did you grow up on ReBoot, Toy Story, or both? Is Toy Story 5 secretly a ReBoot sequel, or am I reaching? Tell me in the comments. Follow, or get rebooted.
